displayName: Míng Yí — Darkening of the Light
articleMarkdown:
# Studying Míng Yí (Darkening of the Light): protecting clear judgment and room to act in adverse conditions

When exposure or advance is unsuitable, first protect important people, information, and judgment, then seek an appropriate way to act.

Sometimes saying everything you know immediately does not help solve a problem; at other times, silence leaves an important problem unseen. Míng Yí describes brightness wounded or concealed, helping us consider caution and uprightness. A hexagram alone cannot confirm that someone is persecuting you, and it does not require silent endurance of actual harm.

## Identity and line order

Míng Yí is hexagram 36 in the traditional King Wen sequence, with symbol ䷣. The lower trigram is Lí ☲ and the upper trigram is Kūn ☷; their traditional images are fire and earth, respectively. Count the lines from the bottom: 初九、六二、九三、六四、六五、上六. A solid line is yang and a broken line is yin. Nine and six in the line labels designate yang and yin; they are not additional line numbers.

```text
━━━━ ━━━━  上六
━━━━ ━━━━  六五
━━━━ ━━━━  六四
━━━━━━━━━  九三
━━━━ ━━━━  六二
━━━━━━━━━  初九
```

## Hexagram statement

明夷：利艱貞。

Original editorial rendering; not a quotation from Legge: Injured brightness: steadfastness amid difficulty is beneficial.

Legge reads Míng Yí as intelligence injured or suppressed, and explains maintaining an appropriate, steadfast course in difficulty. The brief statement emphasizes acknowledging genuine hardship rather than performing bravery.

Today, first establish what needs protection and which actions genuinely help. In matters of safety, rights, or important relationships, a single ancient statement cannot independently decide whether to conceal, disclose, stay, or leave.

References: [zhouyi-36](https://zh.wikisource.org/w/index.php?title=周易/明夷&oldid=10644507), [legge1882-36](https://tianmu.org/good-work-library/confucian/general-texts/the-i-ching-james-legge)

## Interpretations in the Ten Wings

The Commentary on the Judgment and the Commentary on the Images belong to the commentarial collection known as the Yìzhuàn, usually called the Ten Wings. Below, these commentaries are kept separate from the hexagram and line statements, followed by modern learning applications.

The Commentary on the Judgment speaks of brightness entering the earth, illustrating the situation through traditional accounts of King Wen and Jizi. The Commentary on the Images proposes using obscurity while retaining clarity. These are ancient political and ethical interpretations.

This article uses them to consider preserving understanding and proportion under adverse conditions. Caution may include checking material, choosing suitable channels, and seeking trustworthy support. It does not mean abandoning principles or tolerating harm indefinitely.

References: [zhouyi-36](https://zh.wikisource.org/w/index.php?title=周易/明夷&oldid=10644507), [hon-sep](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/chinese-change/)

## The six lines, from bottom to top

### 初九 · Recognize injury and the costs of departure

明夷于飛，垂其翼。君子于行，三日不食，有攸往，主人有言。

Original editorial rendering; not a quotation from Legge: Brightness injured in flight, its wings hanging down. The noble person travels, going three days without food; having somewhere to go, the host has words to say.

Drooping wings, travel, and others' comments form an uneasy beginning. Legge preserves the picture of difficult flight and hardship. Three days without food is part of the textual scene, not advice to the reader.

When an arrangement no longer fits, seriously consider adjustment and its real costs. Preparing necessary support and explaining what can be explained matter more than proving resolve through hunger or exhaustion.

References: [zhouyi-36](https://zh.wikisource.org/w/index.php?title=周易/明夷&oldid=10644507), [legge1882-36](https://tianmu.org/good-work-library/confucian/general-texts/the-i-ching-james-legge)

### 六二 · Harm calls for practical conditions for help

明夷，夷于左股，用拯馬壯，吉。

Original editorial rendering; not a quotation from Legge: Brightness injured: a wound in the left thigh; a strong horse is used for rescue. Good fortune.

The injured left thigh and rescue by a strong horse form a concrete ancient image. Legge's reading emphasizes drawing on strength to get away from harm.

A modern reflection is that willpower alone may not suffice: appropriate help and resources matter. This is neither a diagnosis of bodily injury nor guidance for real rescue procedures.

References: [zhouyi-36](https://zh.wikisource.org/w/index.php?title=周易/明夷&oldid=10644507), [legge1882-36](https://tianmu.org/good-work-library/confucian/general-texts/the-i-ching-james-legge)

### 九三 · Address root problems with care for the pace

明夷于南狩，得其大首，不可疾貞。

Original editorial rendering; not a quotation from Legge: Brightness injured in a southern hunt: the great chief is taken. Do not hurry to put everything right.

The southern hunt and capture of a great chief are images of political hunting or conquest. Legge particularly retains the warning against expecting everything to be set right at once.

In ordinary affairs, finding the main cause still leaves corrections and follow-up to arrange. One identified problem does not justify blaming everyone involved, and ancient actions must not become recommendations for violence.

References: [zhouyi-36](https://zh.wikisource.org/w/index.php?title=周易/明夷&oldid=10644507), [legge1882-36](https://tianmu.org/good-work-library/confucian/general-texts/the-i-ching-james-legge)

### 六四 · Understanding the situation can change the available options

入于左腹，獲明夷之心，于出門庭。

Original editorial rendering; not a quotation from Legge: Entering the left side of the belly, gaining the heart of injured brightness, then going out through gate and courtyard.

Entering the belly, gaining its inner intention, and leaving the courtyard describe a movement from penetration to departure. Legge interprets it within the political setting of an oppressive environment and its ruler.

A modern analogy is establishing why a practice cannot work, then deciding to reduce involvement or use a more suitable channel. The metaphor is not permission to pry into another person's private life or assume you know their thoughts.

References: [zhouyi-36](https://zh.wikisource.org/w/index.php?title=周易/明夷&oldid=10644507), [legge1882-36](https://tianmu.org/good-work-library/confucian/general-texts/the-i-ching-james-legge)

### 六五 · Keep the historical setting without imposing a duty to endure

箕子之明夷，利貞。

Original editorial rendering; not a quotation from Legge: Jizi's injured brightness: steadfastness is beneficial.

Jizi is named directly in the line; the commentary develops his steadfastness in adversity. Legge follows that traditional account. This article does not add unverified historical details.

Today, consider how to preserve important judgments and principles, without requiring anyone to imitate an ancient figure by enduring harm. Actual situations need appropriate support and autonomous choices.

References: [zhouyi-36](https://zh.wikisource.org/w/index.php?title=周易/明夷&oldid=10644507), [legge1882-36](https://tianmu.org/good-work-library/confucian/general-texts/the-i-ching-james-legge)

### 上六 · Power and prominence can also lose direction

不明晦，初登于天，後入于地。

Original editorial rendering; not a quotation from Legge: Not bright, but dark: first rising to heaven, afterward entering the earth.

Brightness and darkness, ascent to heaven and entry into earth create a sharp contrast. Legge reads it as benighted power ultimately losing its former position.

A modern reflection is to check whether success has made you reject facts or disregard others. The line does not predict anyone's inevitable downfall, nor support neglecting present problems while waiting for someone else to be punished.

References: [zhouyi-36](https://zh.wikisource.org/w/index.php?title=周易/明夷&oldid=10644507), [legge1882-36](https://tianmu.org/good-work-library/confucian/general-texts/the-i-ching-james-legge)

## Remaining reliable when source material is disputed

Original modern scenario

A team member prepares a historical introduction containing conflicting accounts. She finds that some content remains unverified, while someone wants to publish immediately. She preserves the sources and differing versions, explains which facts need checking, and proposes publishing only what has been confirmed.

If discussion becomes tense, she chooses a suitable form of communication and asks someone familiar with the material to check it together. She does not publicly speculate about others' motives to prove that she dares to speak.

Míng Yí here supports clarity and proportion without turning caution into a permanent ban on speaking. Evidence and actual communication conditions determine when to continue.

## Misreadings to avoid

- Míng Yí cannot confirm persecution, scheming, or anyone's malicious intent. Whether harm exists requires real evidence and, when needed, trustworthy assistance.

- Drooping wings, a wounded thigh, and going without food are classical images. They provide no basis for health, fasting, or safety decisions and do not glorify suffering or self-sacrifice.

## Three practices

1. Identify one specific thing that needs protecting and explain the real-world reason.

2. Record confirmed facts, information not yet suitable for disclosure, and your own guesses separately.

3. Find a way to communicate or seek help that preserves principles while reducing unnecessary harm.

## Related hexagram

### Jìn — Progress (hexagram-35)

Jìn considers visibility and opportunity; Míng Yí considers conduct when brightness is obscured. Neither visibility nor invisibility is a judgment of worth. The question is how to remain reliable in the circumstances.

## A closing question

While reading Míng Yí, ask: what would help me retain clear judgment and a genuinely possible next step amid difficulty?
